scams.name: Myrtle Beach '$200 Parking Scam' Private-Lot Enforcement
scams.description:
Myrtle Beach has a well-established private-lot ticket-and-tow pattern. Ocean Blvd offers a mix of city-operated metered parking ($2/hour via ParkMobile, with a 2-hour maximum) and privately operated lots advertised with handwritten "$10 all-day" signs. The private lots frequently add unstated "overtime fees" or "after-hours surcharges" of $75–$200, and if you don't pay, they tow your car to industrial tow yards 10 or more miles inland, where release fees run $300–$500, cash only. Some of these private lots are run by former tow-business owners and carry no clear signage. By contrast, a city-operated parking ticket for an expired meter is only $35–$75, never $200 or more.

For older travelers driving to Myrtle Beach, the clean playbook is straightforward. Park at legitimate city-operated lots and metered parking via ParkMobile ($2/hour, 2-hour maximum on Ocean Blvd). Avoid the private lots with handwritten "$10 all-day" signs on the Ocean Blvd side streets — these are ticket-and-tow operations. The Myrtle Beach Boardwalk Paid Parking Lot ($5/day flat rate at 2nd Ave N) is city-operated and legitimate, and parking at Broadway at the Beach and Barefoot Landing is typically free for up to 4 hours with shopping validation. If you receive a "parking ticket" demanding $200 or more in overtime fees, verify it at cityofmyrtlebeach.com before paying, since most are fake or issued by unlicensed private lots. Tow release fees from private operators are often legally disputable in South Carolina — contact the SC Attorney General Consumer Protection division at scag.gov.
scams.avoidance: Park at city lots via ParkMobile ($2/hour) or the Boardwalk Paid Parking lot ($5/day flat). Avoid private Ocean Blvd side-street lots with handwritten signs. Broadway at the Beach and Barefoot Landing are often free with shopping validation. Verify any "ticket" at cityofmyrtlebeach.com before paying. Dispute illegitimate private tows with the SC Attorney General at scag.gov.
scams.location: Myrtle Beach Ocean Blvd metered parking, Grand Strand private parking lots, Broadway at the Beach parking, Barefoot Landing private lots
scams.tldr: Private Ocean Blvd side-street lots with handwritten "$10 all-day" signs tack on $75–$200 "overtime fees," then tow cars 10+ miles inland for cash-only $300–$500 release fees. City meters run $2/hour via ParkMobile, and a genuine city ticket is only $35–$75.

scams.name: Wyndham / Capital Vacations Myrtle Beach Timeshare Presentation Hustle
scams.description:
Myrtle Beach is one of the most aggressive timeshare-sales markets in the United States, home to more than 30 presentation operations, and Wyndham and Capital Vacations draw the most complaints for their presentation tactics. The pattern is consistent. A "free golf package," "free dinner voucher," or "free Ripley's Aquarium tickets" is offered in exchange for a 90-minute presentation, but the presentation actually runs 3–5 hours with relentless pressure to make a $10,000–$40,000 purchase. Capital Vacations markets itself through "travel club" branding that sounds less like a timeshare, and the "concierge" desks in unfamiliar hotel lobbies are often staffed by timeshare salespeople. The maintenance-fee commitment is rarely disclosed upfront — typically $800–$2,400 per year, rising 4–6% annually — and the promised "secondary market" resale value of 30% after 5 years is fiction, since the secondary market is generally $0–$500.

For older travelers in Myrtle Beach, the defensive posture is firm. Refuse all "free gift" offers tied to a "90-minute presentation"; the time cost and pressure tactics make them a net negative. If you do attend, bring a printed "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. If you signed under pressure today, South Carolina grants a 5-day right of rescission for timeshare contracts — cancel immediately by certified mail. If you signed more than 5 days ago, the SC Attorney General Consumer Protection division (scconsumer.gov) may be able to help. Avoid "timeshare exit" companies charging $5,000–$15,000, as many are the same operators rebranded. Report high-pressure tactics from Wyndham, Capital Vacations, Bluegreen, Westgate, and Hilton Grand Vacations to the SC Attorney General and the BBB.
scams.avoidance: Refuse all "free gift" offers tied to a 90-minute presentation. If you attend, bring an "I will not sign anything today" rule and stick to it. If you signed, use South Carolina's 5-day right of rescission via certified mail immediately. Contact SC Attorney General Consumer Protection at scconsumer.gov. Avoid "exit" companies charging $5,000 or more — use the state AG instead.
scams.location: Wyndham Myrtle Beach Resort sales offices, Capital Vacations Beach House Resort, Ocean Blvd hotel-lobby 'concierge' desks, Broadway at the Beach mall promoter kiosks
scams.tldr: A "free golf package" or "free Ripley's tickets" lures you into a presentation billed at 90 minutes but lasting 3–5 hours, with pressure to spend $10,000–$40,000. Undisclosed maintenance fees run $800–$2,400 a year, and the promised resale value is essentially worthless.

scams.name: Myrtle Beach Boardwalk Pizza-Flyer & Kid-Pressure Panhandling Scam
scams.description:
The Myrtle Beach Boardwalk has a specific solicitation pattern. Adult handlers employ children, ages 8 to 14, to hand pizza-restaurant flyers to tourists. The flyer promotes a real pizza restaurant, but the child then asks for a "$2–$5 tip for the flyer," and tourists feel pressured to pay because they feel sorry for the kids. The handler waits nearby and collects all the tips. In effect, this is exploited-child panhandling dressed up as flyer delivery. Related schemes appear in the same area: "beach chair rental" at $15–$25 per day from unauthorized vendors, even though hotels typically include free chairs; "henna tattoo" vendors who apply artwork unsolicited and then demand $20–$40; and "photographer" touts charging $20–$40 for unsolicited beach photos. Travelers also widely report broader quality concerns about the Boardwalk.

For older travelers on the Myrtle Beach Boardwalk, the defensive playbook is simple. Refuse all flyer hand-offs from children — a firm "no thank you" and keep walking. Do not give cash to kids for flyers; you are funding adult exploitation, not helping the child. If you want pizza, look up the actual restaurant independently and visit it directly. Refuse all "beach chair rental" from unauthorized vendors — if your hotel doesn't include chairs, Oceanic Vacation Rentals and official hotel rental desks are legitimate. Refuse unsolicited "henna" and "photography" approaches, which are payment-extraction setups. If you are concerned about a child's welfare, report it to the Horry County Department of Social Services (843-915-5525) rather than handing over cash, which only perpetuates the pattern. For aggressive solicitation, call the Myrtle Beach PD non-emergency line (843-918-1382).
scams.avoidance: Refuse all flyer hand-offs from children — a firm "no thank you" and keep walking. Don't give cash to kids; it funds adult exploitation, not the child. Look up pizza restaurants independently and visit directly. Use hotel-provided chairs or Oceanic Vacation Rentals for legitimate beach chairs. Refuse unsolicited henna or photography, which are payment-extraction setups.
scams.location: Myrtle Beach Boardwalk (Ocean Blvd, Plyler Park to Pier 14), Broadway at the Beach pedestrian strip, Grand Strand beach entrance points
scams.tldr: Adult handlers send children to hand tourists pizza flyers, then have the kids ask for a "$2–$5 tip" while the handler pockets the money. Watch too for unauthorized $15–$25 beach-chair rentals, unsolicited $20–$40 henna, and $20–$40 photo touts.

scams.name: MYR Airport Rideshare Availability & Taxi Overcharge
scams.description:
MYR is 3–5 miles from most Grand Strand hotels, and the legitimate fares are predictable: Uber or Lyft run $12–$22 when available, and a licensed taxi with a meter runs $18–$28. Several scam variants work this route. Drivers at baggage claim offer a "flat $35–$50" to Ocean Blvd hotels when the legitimate fare is $12–$28; "limo" touts quote $60 or more for standard trips; Uber and Lyft availability tightens during peak cruise weekends and the Sun Fun festival, and drivers may cancel after confirming; "shared shuttle" touts offer a "beach shuttle" at $25 per person against an $8 Uber Pool; and fake operators using names like "Coastal Tours Shuttle" disappear once they have your payment.

For older travelers arriving at MYR, the clean playbook starts at the designated rideshare pickup. Take Uber or Lyft with a fare screenshot when available ($12–$22 to most Grand Strand hotels), or a licensed metered taxi from the official queue ($18–$28 to Ocean Blvd). During peak events — Labor Day, Sun Fun, spring break, and Bike Week — Uber availability can be spotty, so reserve in advance via Uber Reserve or call Coastal Cab (843-444-9830) for a confirmed licensed taxi. Avoid drivers soliciting at baggage claim with "flat" rates 50% or more above the metered fare. For airport-to-hotel shuttles, book only through your hotel's official shuttle service, not a third-party operator like "Coastal Tours Shuttle" or other unverified names. Never pay a cash tip beyond the Uber app total, since app tips are already processed.
scams.avoidance: Take Uber or Lyft at the designated pickup with a fare screenshot ($12–$22). Use a licensed metered taxi at the official queue ($18–$28 to Ocean Blvd). Reserve rideshare ahead for peak events (Labor Day, Sun Fun, Bike Week). Call Coastal Cab for a reliable licensed taxi at 843-444-9830. Book shuttles only through your hotel's official service, never third-party operators.
scams.location: Myrtle Beach International Airport (MYR), baggage claim taxi solicitors, rideshare pickup zones, 'shuttle' touts
scams.tldr: Baggage-claim drivers push "flat $35–$50" rates to Ocean Blvd hotels when the real fare is $12–$28, and limo and shuttle touts quote far more. Rideshare availability tightens during Sun Fun, Bike Week, and cruise weekends, so reserve ahead.

scams.name: Myrtle Beach 'Where to Avoid' — Broadway at the Beach & Tourist-Trap Venues
scams.description:
Myrtle Beach has its share of tourist-trap venues, and as of 2025 there are ongoing reports of employee-exploitation problems at Myrtle Waves Water Park — relevant to tourists because the park has reduced service quality, staff shortages, and continuing complaints. The common tourist-trap patterns are easy to spot once you know them. Dining venues at Broadway at the Beach charge 40–70% above comparable non-tourist Myrtle Beach restaurants. An "all-you-can-eat seafood buffet" at $49 or more per person serves the lowest-grade imported product. A "VIP beach package" hotel upsell at $300 or more per day covers a beach chair (free at most hotels), a beach umbrella ($15 retail), and "priority seating" that doesn't exist. A Ripley's Aquarium plus Myrtle Waves plus WonderWorks combo package at $140 or more per person offers no real discount, since direct pricing is $68 + $45 + $29 = $142. And tourist-area mini golf at $20 or more per person is steep next to Topsail Mini Golf at $10.

For older travelers in Myrtle Beach, the honest playbook points elsewhere. For authentic Lowcountry seafood, skip the Broadway at the Beach dining and drive 15 minutes to the Hot Fish Club (Murrells Inlet, $18–$35, genuine local seafood) or Drunken Jack's (Murrells Inlet MarshWalk, $20–$42). For family attractions, Ripley's Aquarium ($29.99 direct at ripleys.com) and Myrtle Beach State Park ($5 per person admission, with a 1-mile nature boardwalk) are fair value. Avoid Myrtle Waves Water Park given the 2025 community concerns about staffing and quality — Wild Water & Wheels in North Myrtle Beach is a better choice. For outlet shopping, Tanger Outlets Myrtle Beach delivers $50–$75 in average savings on brand-name items. For mini golf, Jungle Lagoon and Hawaiian Rumble are both well reviewed. And the Myrtle Beach Boardwalk and Ocean Blvd itself are free to walk — there is no "access fee," despite the occasional tout's claim.
scams.avoidance: For seafood, go to the Hot Fish Club or Drunken Jack's in Murrells Inlet ($18–$42). Buy Ripley's Aquarium tickets direct at ripleys.com ($29.99) and visit Myrtle Beach State Park ($5). For a water park, choose Wild Water & Wheels in North Myrtle Beach. For outlet shopping, use Tanger Outlets Myrtle Beach for genuine discounts. For mini golf, pick the well-reviewed Jungle Lagoon or Hawaiian Rumble.
scams.location: Broadway at the Beach dining strip, Ocean Blvd tourist restaurants, Barefoot Landing overpriced venues, Myrtle Waves Park + similar attractions
scams.tldr: Broadway at the Beach restaurants run 40–70% above local spots, "VIP beach packages" charge $300+ a day for free amenities, and combo attraction tickets bundle no real discount. Murrells Inlet seafood and direct attraction pricing are far better value.

scams.name: Myrtle Beach Hotel Resort Fee & STR Off-Platform Booking Fraud
scams.description:
Myrtle Beach's Grand Strand hosts more than 450 hotels and over 14,000 vacation condos, making it the largest beach-lodging market on the East Coast. With that scale come several scam variants. A "resort fee" of $15–$35 per night is added at check-in rather than at booking, ostensibly covering "WiFi, pool, and beach chair" — often items that are already free. A "parking fee" of $15–$25 per night appears at hotels that advertise "free parking," and a "mandatory towel rental" runs $8–$15 per day. Off-platform "oceanfront Airbnb" listings ask for Zelle or Venmo at "$100 below market," but the listings are fake, frequently cloned from Airbnb onto Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace. "Last-minute Grand Strand condo" ads run during peak seasons (June through August, Memorial Day, and Labor Day) with Zelle-only payment, and a "cleaning fee" of $150–$400 turns up on 2-night stays that should cost $50–$150.

For older travelers booking Myrtle Beach accommodation, the protective playbook is clear. When comparing hotels, add the resort fee and parking to the headline rate. Book short-term rentals only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment — never Zelle, Venmo, or wire. Verified Myrtle Beach condo operators include Condo-World (condo-world.com), Elliott Beach Rentals (elliottbeachrentals.com), Oceanfront Vacation Rentals (oceanfrontmyrtlebeach.com), and Beach Vacations Myrtle Beach, all of which hold SC business licenses. For Memorial Day, the Fourth of July, and Labor Day, book 4–6 months ahead. Legitimate brand hotels include the Marriott Resort & Spa at Grande Dunes, Embassy Suites Myrtle Beach Oceanfront, DoubleTree Resort Myrtle Beach, and Hilton Myrtle Beach Resort. If a "resort fee" was not disclosed in your online booking, dispute it at check-in and with your credit card. And check resortfeechecker.com before booking for all-in pricing.
scams.avoidance: Add resort and parking fees to the headline hotel rate when comparing. Book short-term rentals only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment. Use verified operators like Condo-World, Elliott Beach Rentals, and Oceanfront Vacation Rentals. Book 4–6 months ahead for Memorial Day, the Fourth of July, and Labor Day. Check resortfeechecker.com for all-in pricing.
scams.location: Ocean Blvd oceanfront hotels (Myrtle Beach + North Myrtle Beach), Grand Strand resort properties, Cherry Grove + Surfside Beach STRs
scams.tldr: Hotels tack on undisclosed "resort," "parking," and "towel" fees at check-in, while fake off-platform condo listings demand Zelle or Venmo at "$100 below market." Book only through major platforms and add hidden fees to the headline rate when comparing.
